claim: Degeneration of cholinergic neurons and a low tone of ACh correlate with memory impairment in humans and rodents.
source: On one hand, degeneration of cholinergic neurons and a low tone of ACh correlate with memory impairment in humans and rodents (Bartus, 2000; Berger-Sweeney et al., 2001; Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartus, 2000; Berger-Sweeney et al., 2001; Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011

claim: Drugs blocking ACh degradation ameliorate memory impairment in Alzheimer's disease.
source: drugs blocking ACh degradation ameliorate memory impairment in Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Ehret and Chamberlin, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ehret and Chamberlin, 2015

claim: Extensive lesions of the medial septum produce learning deficits.
source: Moreover, extensive lesions of the medial septum (MS), where the cholinergic neurons projecting to the hippocampus are located, produce learning deficits (Hepler et al., 1985)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hepler et al., 1985

claim: Selective lesions of MS cholinergic neurons have relatively little impact on learning and memory.
source: On the other hand, selective lesions of MS cholinergic neurons, which account for ~5% of neurons in the MS, have relatively little impact on learning and memory (for review, see Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Solari and Hangya, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles by Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Solari and Hangya, 2018

claim: ACh levels vary during memory formation.
source: A reason for these apparently conflicting results may lie in the fact that memory formation is a dynamic process during which ACh levels vary (Fadda et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fadda et al., 2000

claim: Long-term memory forms in two stages: first, neuronal activity produces a labile trace, then a delayed potentiation of the same synapses forms a long-lasting memory trace.
source: In an influential model, Buzsáki, 1989 suggested that long-term memory forms in two stages: first, neuronal activity produces a labile trace, then a delayed potentiation of the same synapses forms a long-lasting memory trace.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buzsáki, 1989

claim: Phase-amplitude-coupled theta (5–12 Hz)-gamma (30–100 Hz) oscillations occur during exploratory behaviors in rodents.
source: In rodents, phase-amplitude-coupled theta (5–12 Hz)-gamma (30–100 Hz) oscillations (Csicsvari et al., 2003) occur during exploratory behaviors
evidence: Supported by citation to Csicsvari et al., 2003

claim: Large-amplitude sharp waves combined with high-frequency ripples (sharp wave ripples [SWRs]) occur during immobility and slow-wave sleep.
source: while large-amplitude sharp waves combined with high-frequency ripples (sharp wave ripples [SWRs]) (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Csicsvari et al., 2000) occur during immobility and slow-wave sleep
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Csicsvari et al., 2000

claim: Theta/gamma oscillations and SWRs are mutually exclusive network states.
source: These two network states are mutually exclusive (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Buzsáki, 1986; Csicsvari et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Buzsáki, 1986; Csicsvari et al., 2000

claim: Memory encoding is associated with theta/gamma oscillations while memory consolidation relies on SWR activity.
source: it was suggested that memory encoding is associated with theta/gamma oscillations while memory consolidation relies on SWR activity (O'Neill et al., 2010; Colgin, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Neill et al., 2010; Colgin, 2013

claim: Cholinergic activation ex vivo induces a slow gamma rhythm in hippocampal CA3 primarily by activating M1 muscarinic receptors.
source: In hippocampal CA3, cholinergic activation ex vivo induces a slow gamma rhythm primarily by activating M1 muscarinic receptors (Fisahn et al., 1998; Betterton et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fisahn et al., 1998; Betterton et al., 2017

claim: Cholinergic activation in vivo promotes theta/gamma oscillations and suppresses ripple oscillations in CA1 through the activation of M2/M4 muscarinic receptors.
source: while in the CA1, cholinergic activation in vivo promotes theta/gamma oscillations and suppresses ripple oscillations through the activation of M2/M4 muscarinic receptors (Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020

claim: There is a high cholinergic tone during exploration, promoting theta activity, and a lower cholinergic tone during subsequent rest, permitting SWRs.
source: Evidence from microdialysis and electrophysiology experiments shows a high cholinergic tone during exploration, promoting theta activity, and a lower cholinergic tone during subsequent rest, permitting SWRs (Fadda et al., 2000; Giovannini et al., 2001; Fadel, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fadda et al., 2000; Giovannini et al., 2001; Fadel, 2011

claim: Disruption of cholinergic activity at different stages of learning and memory impairs performance in memory tasks.
source: Disruption of cholinergic activity at different stages of learning and memory impairs performance in memory tasks (for review, see Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Solari and Hangya, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles by Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Solari and Hangya, 2018

claim: 65% of ChAT+ cells in the medial septum of ChAT-Ai32 mice are YFP+.
source: In sections sampled from two mice, 98 out of 150 ChAT+ cells counted were YFP+ (YFP+/ChAT+=65%)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunostaining quantification

claim: 100% of YFP+ cells in the medial septum of ChAT-Ai32 mice are ChAT+.
source: In independently sampled sections, 111 out of 111 YFP+ cells counted were ChAT+ (ChAT+/YFP+=100%)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunostaining quantification

claim: Local light delivery (50 ms pulses at 10 Hz) in the MS resulted in an increase in multi-unit activity.
source: Local light delivery (50 ms pulses at 10 Hz) resulted in an increase in multi-unit activity (baseline spike frequency: 7.9 ± 2.8 Hz vs. spike frequency during light delivery: 22.7 ± 7.3 Hz, two-tailed Wilcoxon matched pair signed-rank test: p=0.03; n = 6 recordings from two mice; Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multi-unit recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1B

claim: Sharp wave ripples have been reported at the reward location of different spatial navigation tasks.
source: Previous studies have reported sharp wave ripples at the reward location of different spatial navigation tasks (O'Neill et al., 2006; Dupret et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Neill et al., 2006; Dupret et al., 2010

claim: ChAT-Ai32 mice in the 'goal' group took significantly longer to reach learning criterion compared to the 'no stimulation' group.
source: Post hoc tests indicated that the ChAT-Ai32 'goal' group was delayed at learning the task compared to the ChAT-Ai32 'no stimulation' group (4.5 ± 0.3 vs. 2.9 ± 0.3 days, Dunn test with Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons: p=0.002, BF10 = 45)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing and statistical analysis

claim: ChAT-Ai32 mice in the 'goal' group took significantly longer to reach learning criterion compared to the 'navigation' group.
source: Similarly, the ChAT-Ai32 'goal' group was delayed compared to the ChAT-Ai32 'navigation' group (4.5 ± 0.3 vs. 3.1 ± 0.4 days, p=0.05, BF10 = 4.4)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing and statistical analysis

claim: There was no learning difference between the 'goal' and 'no stimulation' groups of wild-type mice.
source: We did not observe any learning difference between the 'goal' and 'no stimulation' groups of this control WT mice cohort (goal: 3.0 ± 0.37 days; no stimulation: 3.4 ± 0.37 days; one-way ANOVA F(1, 14) = 0.34, p=0.57; Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2F

claim: Cholinergic activation in the goal zone for as short as 50 s slows learning of the appetitive Y-maze task.
source: Our results show that cholinergic activation in the goal zone for as short as 50 s (95% percentile of stimulation duration) slows learning of the appetitive Y-maze task.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing

claim: Optogenetic stimulation during navigation or throughout the maze had no significant effect on task acquisition.
source: In contrast, optogenetic stimulation during navigation or throughout the maze had no significant effect on task acquisition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing

claim: Cholinergic activation did not affect the time mice spent at the goal location.
source: The cholinergic activation did not overtly affect the behavior once the mice were at the goal location: we did not detect any effect of the laser on the time the mice spent at the goal location (linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 78)=0.01, p=0.94, laser effect: F(1, 78)=0.1, p=0.73)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral observations and statistical analysis

claim: Theta power peaked in the central section of the maze where the mice ran the fastest.
source: The theta power (5–12 Hz) peaked in the central section of the maze where the mice ran the fastest (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings, shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Theta power was reduced at the goal location in rewarded trials.
source: Theta power (5–12 Hz) peaked in the central section of the maze where the mice ran the fastest (Figure 3A,B) and was reduced at the goal location in rewarded trials (Figure 3B, right panel)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings, shown in Figure 3B

claim: Light did not affect the relative theta power differently in the ChAT-GFP and ChAT-ChR2 mice.
source: Light did not affect the relative theta power differently in the ChAT-GFP and ChAT-ChR2 mice (linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 5)=0.01, p=0.94, Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3E

claim: Theta power increased by 16 ± 3% in both ChAT-GFP and ChAT-ChR2 mouse groups during laser stimulation.
source: However, theta power increased by 16 ± 3% in both mouse groups indiscriminately (laser effect: F(1, 5)=6.9, p=0.05), suggesting another, non-specific effect of the laser on theta power.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis

claim: Spectral peak frequency in the theta band was not significantly affected by the stimulation.
source: Spectral peak frequency in the theta band was not significantly affected by the stimulation (linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 5)=1.3, p=0.31, laser effect: F(1, 5)=3.5, p=0.12, Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3F

claim: Optogenetic stimulation did not affect relative slow gamma power.
source: Similarly, quantification of the relative slow gamma power indicated no effect of the stimulation (linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 6)=1.7, p=0.24, laser effect: F(1, 6)=0.1, p=0.77, Figure 3G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3G

claim: The laser reduced the aperiodic component of the PSD in the 3–15 Hz range differently in ChAT-GFP and ChAT-ChR2 mice.
source: The only effect of the laser that affected PSD of the ChAT-GFP and ChAT-ChR2 mice differently was a reduced aperiodic component of the PSD in the 3–15 Hz range (linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 135)=29, p=10−7, Figure 3H)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3H

claim: Activation of septal cholinergic neurons suppresses CA1 SWRs.
source: Previous studies have shown that activation of septal cholinergic neurons suppresses CA1 SWRs (Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2020

claim: SWRs occurred at the start and the goal locations during the Y-maze task.
source: The SWRs occurred at the start and the goal locations (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings, shown in Figure 4B

claim: SWRs were detected in significantly more rewarded than unrewarded trials.
source: We detected SWRs in significantly more rewarded than unrewarded trials (82 ± 7% of rewarded non-stimulated trials vs. 32 ± 13% of unrewarded non-stimulated trials, paired t-test on percentages per animal: p=0.02, n = 7 animals, Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4C

claim: SWR incidence did not change significantly between early and late learning.
source: We did not observe any significant difference between early (before day 5) and late learning (linear mixed-effects model, effect of early vs. late learning: F(1, 110)=0.3, p=0.58, Figure 4D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4D

claim: Optogenetic stimulation reduced SWR incidence at the goal location in ChAT-ChR2 mice by 52 ± 7%.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation had a significantly different effect in the ChAT-GFP and the ChAT-ChR2 mice (log-linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction, F(1, 42) = 4.5, p=0.04, Figure 4E), whose SWR incidence at the goal location was reduced by 52 ± 7% from 0.06 ± 0.01 to 0.03 ± 0.01 Hz (post hoc test: t(44) = 4.2, p=0.001, Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4E

claim: Spectral peak frequency of SWRs was not affected by the stimulation.
source: Spectral peak frequency of SWRs was not affected by the stimulation (frequency: 168 ± 2 Hz; linear mixed-effects model for non-stimulated trials, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 3.6)=0.02, p=0.88, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: SWR duration was not affected by the stimulation.
source: nor was the SWR duration (duration: 37 ± 1 ms; log-linear mixed-effects model for non-stimulated trials, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 148)=0.1, p=0.76, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: There are at least two distinct forms of theta oscillations in the hippocampus, only one of which is dependent on cholinergic receptors and can be observed during sleep.
source: However, there are at least two distinct forms of theta oscillations in the hippocampus, only one of which is dependent on cholinergic receptors and can be observed during sleep (Kramis et al., 1975)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kramis et al., 1975

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons reduced SWR incidence throughout the stimulation in ChAT-ChR2 mice but not in ChAT-GFP mice during sleep.
source: Optogenetic stimulation reduced the SWR incidence throughout the stimulation in ChAT-ChR2 mice but not in ChAT-GFP mice (Figure 5A–C). SWR incidence in ChAT-ChR2 mice was reduced from 0.21 ± 0.01 to 0.03 ± 0.01 Hz (85 ± 3% reduction, linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 22)=47, p=10−6, n = 369 epochs from 10 animals; post hoc test for laser effect in ChAT-ChR2: t(86) = 9.7, p=10−14, Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5A–C

claim: Optogenetic stimulation during sleep did not change the spectral peak frequency of SWRs.
source: The stimulation did not change the spectral peak frequency of the SWRs of 168 ± 1 Hz (mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 262)=0.51, p=0.48, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Optogenetic stimulation during sleep did not change ripple duration.
source: nor ripple duration of 38 ± 0.3 ms (log-linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 28)=0.9, p=0.35, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Optogenetic activation of MS cholinergic neurons almost completely suppresses SWRs during sleep in the CA1.
source: Hence, our results confirm that optogenetic activation of MS cholinergic neurons almost completely suppresses SWRs during sleep in the CA1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons causes a reduction of the PSD across the full frequency range in sleeping mice.
source: We observed a reduction of the PSD across the full frequency range upon light stimulation (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), as reported previously in freely behaving mice (Vandecasteele et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and citation to Vandecasteele et al., 2014, shown in Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Broadband power of the aperiodic component decreased with light stimulation in the ChAT-ChR2 but not in the ChAT-GFP mice during sleep.
source: Broadband power of the aperiodic component decreased with light stimulation in the ChAT-ChR2 but not in the ChAT-GFP mice (linear mixed-effects model on area under curve [AUC] of estimated aperiodic component on PSD log-log plot, significant mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 4.6)=22, p=0.006, n = 369 epochs from 10 mice; AUC significantly decreased from −5.96 ± 0.04 to −6.23 ± 0.04, post hoc test for laser effect in ChAT-ChR2: t(7.1) = 10.1, p=10−4, Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6D

claim: Optogenetic stimulation increased relative theta power by 51 ± 9% in ChAT-ChR2 mice during sleep.
source: Optogenetic stimulation had a significantly different effect in the ChAT-GFP and the ChAT-ChR2 animals on the relative theta power (log-linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 4.8)=7.3, p=0.04, n = 368 epochs with theta peak from 10 animals, Figure 6E). In the ChAT-ChR2 mice, the power increased by 51 ± 9% (post hoc test: t(9) = 4.8, p=0.01)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6E

claim: Optogenetic stimulation decreased the spectral peak frequency in the theta band from 7.7 ± 0.2 to 7.2 ± 0.1 Hz in ChAT-ChR2 mice during sleep.
source: and the spectral peak frequency in the theta band decreased from 7.7 ± 0.2 to 7.2 ± 0.1 Hz (log-linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 4.8)=7.3, p=0.04, Figure 6F, post hoc test: t(30) = 4.5, p=0.001)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6F

claim: Optogenetic stimulation increased oscillations in the slow gamma band (25–45 Hz) by 30 ± 4% in ChAT-ChR2 mice during sleep.
source: The stimulation also increased by 30 ± 4% oscillations in the slow gamma band (25–45 Hz) (log-linear mixed-effects model: mouse group–laser interaction: F(1, 232)=26, p=10−6, n = 338 epochs with slow gamma peak from 10 animals, post hoc test for laser effect in ChAT-ChR2: t(295) = −8.2, p=10−14, Figure 6G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6G

claim: The spectral peak frequency in the slow gamma did not significantly change during optogenetic stimulation in sleep.
source: while the spectral peak frequency in the slow gamma of 38 ± 1 Hz did not significantly change (linear mixed-effects model, mouse group–laser interaction: F(1,10) = 0.4, p=0.57)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and statistical analysis

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons promotes theta-gamma oscillations in the CA1 of sleeping mice.
source: Our results demonstrate that in sleeping mice, optogenetic stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons promotes theta-gamma oscillations in the CA1, an effect that was not seen in awake mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep

claim: MS cholinergic activation at the goal location, but not during navigation, impairs spatial memory formation.
source: We found that: (1) MS cholinergic activation at the goal location, but not during navigation, impairs spatial memory formation
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing

claim: MS cholinergic stimulation at the reward location reduces SWR incidence.
source: (2) MS cholinergic stimulation at the reward location reduces SWR incidence
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings

claim: Cholinergic stimulation almost completely suppresses SWRs in sleeping animals and suppresses SWRs by about one half in awake, behaving animals.
source: Our results indicate that cholinergic stimulation almost completely suppresses SWRs in sleeping animals and suppresses SWRs by about one half in awake, behaving animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and awake behavior

claim: SWRs at the rewarded locations are thought to be crucial for learning.
source: SWRs at the rewarded locations are thought to be crucial for learning (Dupret et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupret et al., 2010

claim: Disruption of SWRs in the first 15–60 min following training impairs learning of spatial navigation tasks.
source: There is evidence to suggest that CA1 SWRs, which occur during low cholinergic activity, play a crucial role in memory formation: disruption of SWRs in the first 15–60 min following training impairs learning of spatial navigation tasks (Girardeau et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Girardeau et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010

claim: Disruption or prolongation of SWRs during the continuous alternation task impairs or improves learning respectively.
source: while their disruption or prolongation during the continuous alternation task impairs or improves learning respectively (Jadhav et al., 2012; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Jadhav et al., 2012; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019

claim: SWRs stabilize spatial representations of the CA1 place cells supporting navigation toward the newly learned goals.
source: These SWRs stabilize spatial representations of the CA1 place cells supporting navigation toward the newly learned goals (Roux et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Roux et al., 2017

claim: SWRs are predictive of performance in a spatial memory task.
source: and are predictive of performance in a spatial memory task (O'Neill et al., 2006; Dupret et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Neill et al., 2006; Dupret et al., 2010

claim: During SWRs, sequences of neuronal activation are replayed in both forward and reverse order.
source: During these SWRs, sequences of neuronal activation are replayed in both forward and reverse order (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Csicsvari et al., 2007; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Ambrose et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Foster and Wilson, 2006; Csicsvari et al., 2007; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Ambrose et al., 2016

claim: Selective disruption of SWRs at the reward zone did not affect rats' performance in the inbound phase of the W-maze task.
source: However, selective disruption of SWRs at the reward zone did not affect rats' performance in the inbound phase of the W-maze task (Jadhav et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jadhav et al., 2012

claim: Learning can be affected by the interruption of SWRs during post-learning sleep.
source: Because learning can be affected by the interruption of SWRs during post-learning sleep (Girardeau et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Girardeau et al., 2009

claim: MS cholinergic neurons discharge at a maximal rate when the animal is running.
source: MS cholinergic neurons discharge at a maximal rate when the animal is running (Ma et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2020

claim: Cholinergic tone and MS cholinergic neuron discharge are at their lowest during slow-wave sleep and wake immobility.
source: Conversely, cholinergic tone and MS cholinergic neuron discharge are at their lowest during slow-wave sleep and wake immobility, which are associated with the highest ripple incidence (Fadda et al., 2000; Ma et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fadda et al., 2000; Ma et al., 2020

claim: Stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons reduces SWR incidence in both awake behaving animals and naturally sleeping animals.
source: In accordance with these observations, we found that stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons reduces SWR incidence in both awake behaving animals and naturally sleeping animals, consistent with previous reports (Figures 4 and 5; Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings and citations to Vandecasteele et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020, shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons of sleeping mice causes an apparent decrease of the PSD across the entire frequency spectrum.
source: We observed that stimulation of MS cholinergic neurons of sleeping mice causes an apparent decrease of the PSD across the entire frequency spectrum (Figure 6). A similar effect was reported previously for anesthetized and freely behaving animals (Vandecasteele et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep and citation to Vandecasteele et al., 2014, shown in Figure 6

claim: There are two distinct mechanisms of theta oscillations in the hippocampus, an atropine-sensitive and an atropine-resistant component.
source: Pharmacological evidence in vivo indicates that there are two distinct mechanisms of theta oscillations in the hippocampus, an atropine-sensitive and an atropine-resistant component (Petsche et al., 1962; Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Petsche et al., 1962; Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2013

claim: The atropine-sensitive component is mediated by the combination of cholinergic and GABAergic neurons in the MS.
source: The atropine-sensitive component is mediated by the combination of cholinergic and GABAergic neurons in the MS (Buzsáki, 2002; Manseau et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002; Manseau et al., 2008

claim: Atropine-sensitive theta is slower than the atropine-insensitive theta rhythm, which is generated primarily by the entorhinal cortex.
source: and is slower than the atropine-insensitive theta rhythm, which is generated primarily by the entorhinal cortex (Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2013

claim: Atropine-sensitive theta was best detected in the anesthetized animal, while atropine-insensitive theta was shown to predominate in the running animal.
source: Moreover, atropine-sensitive theta was best detected in the anesthetized animal, while atropine-insensitive theta was shown to predominate in the running animal (Kramis et al., 1975; Newman et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kramis et al., 1975; Newman et al., 2013

claim: MS cholinergic stimulation in sleeping mice shifted the spectral peak in the theta band to a lower frequency.
source: Consistent with this division, MS cholinergic stimulation in sleeping mice, in addition to increasing theta power, shifted the spectral peak in the theta band to a lower frequency (Figure 6F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LFP recordings during sleep, shown in Figure 6F

claim: Loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain is one of the hallmarks of AD.
source: Loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain is one of the hallmarks of AD (Whitehouse et al., 1982; Bowen et al., 1982)
evidence: Supported by citations to Whitehouse et al., 1982; Bowen et al., 1982

claim: AD is associated with a reduction of ACh transporter expression in most cortical and subcortical areas.
source: which is also associated with a reduction of ACh transporter expression in most cortical and subcortical areas (Davies and Maloney, 1976)
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies and Maloney, 1976

claim: MS cholinergic neuronal loss occurs in both healthy aging and AD brain.
source: However, the association between the loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons and AD is not completely clear (Mesulam, 2004), and a growing body of anatomical and functional studies suggests that MS cholinergic neuronal loss occurs in both healthy aging and AD brain (Schliebs and Arendt, 2011; Hampel et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mesulam, 2004; Schliebs and Arendt, 2011; Hampel et al., 2018

claim: Drugs targeting the cholinergic systems have shown limited beneficial effects on cognitive deficits of aging and AD.
source: However, so far, drugs targeting the cholinergic systems have shown limited beneficial effects on cognitive deficits of aging and AD, but the reasons why are not entirely clear (Farlow et al., 2010; Ehret and Chamberlin, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farlow et al., 2010; Ehret and Chamberlin, 2015

claim: Cholinesterase inhibitors prolong cholinergic activity by ~100 times and increase the basal cholinergic tone in the absence of spontaneous activity.
source: Cholinesterase inhibitors prolong cholinergic activity by ~100 times and increase the basal cholinergic tone in the absence of spontaneous activity (Hay et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hay et al., 2016

claim: The cholinergic tone is high during exploration, which maintains the 'online' hippocampal state dominated by theta and gamma oscillations.
source: In rodents, the cholinergic tone is high during exploration, which maintains the 'online' hippocampal state dominated by theta and gamma oscillations (Buzsáki, 1989; Fadda et al., 2000; Giovannini et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzsáki, 1989; Fadda et al., 2000; Giovannini et al., 2001

claim: Artificially increasing ACh release for as short a time as 50 s during a low cholinergic state is sufficient to impair task acquisition.
source: This could impair memory formation as our results suggest that artificially increasing ACh release for as short a time as 50 s during a low cholinergic state is sufficient to impair task acquisition (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing, shown in Figure 2

claim: Enhancing cholinergic activity during the 'online' state did not bring beneficial effects to memory formation.
source: Moreover, enhancing cholinergic activity during the 'online' state did not bring beneficial effects to memory formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing

claim: Appropriate timing of cholinergic modulation is crucial in learning and memory.
source: Thus, our results suggest that suboptimal timing of cholinergic activity impairs long-term memory formation and supports the idea that appropriate timing of cholinergic modulation is crucial in learning and memory (Micheau and Marighetto, 2011)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Micheau and Marighetto, 2011
